sidebarLabel: PTR, SRV, Zone Transfer & Subdomain Enumeration
title: PTR, SRV, Zone Transfer, and Subdomain Enumeration: The Complete Picture
content:
Four more concepts that complete your DNS intelligence toolkit. Two are record types. One is a protocol feature. One is the technique that ties everything together.

---

**The PTR Record: The Reverse Directory**

Every DNS record type you have learned so far goes from name to number: you give DNS a domain name, DNS gives you an IP address. PTR records work in the opposite direction.

A PTR record (Pointer record) maps an IP address back to a hostname.

**The analogy**: If A records are the phone book — you look up a name to get a number — PTR records are the reverse phone book. You already have a number and want to know whose name it belongs to.

**Why it exists**: Mail servers use PTR records as part of spam prevention. When mail server A receives an email from IP address 45.77.180.10 claiming to be from mail.meridian-financial.com, the receiving server checks whether the PTR record for 45.77.180.10 actually confirms 'mail.meridian-financial.com.' If the PTR record does not match — or does not exist — the email is more likely to be flagged as spam.

PTR records live in a special DNS zone: the in-addr.arpa zone. The IP address is reversed and appended with in-addr.arpa. So the PTR record for 45.77.180.10 is stored as: 10.180.77.45.in-addr.arpa.

**Reconnaissance value**: Run a PTR lookup on any IP address you discover and you will often get a hostname back. That hostname frequently tells you exactly what the server does:
— 'vpn-gateway-01.meridian-financial.com' → the VPN server
— 'mail01.meridian-financial.com' → the primary mail server
— 'db-primary.meridian-financial.com' → the primary database
— 'jenkins.internal.company.com' → a CI/CD server

Internal hostnames in PTR records sometimes reveal naming conventions and infrastructure roles that are not visible in forward DNS at all.

---

**The SRV Record: The Services Catalog (Introduction Only)**

SRV records (Service records) tell DNS-aware applications which server and port handle a specific service for a domain.

**The analogy**: If the building's public directory says 'Reception is at the main entrance,' the SRV record is the professional services catalog in the lobby: 'Legal consultation: Suite 405, Building B, available 9am–5pm weekdays.'

**Format**: _service._protocol.domain → priority weight port target
Example: _sip._tcp.meridian-financial.com → 10 20 5060 sip.meridian-financial.com

This means: the SIP VoIP service for meridian-financial.com runs on sip.meridian-financial.com, port 5060, over TCP.

**Common SRV record services you might encounter**:
— _sip._tcp or _sips._tcp → VoIP/telephony infrastructure
— _xmpp-client._tcp → XMPP instant messaging
— _autodiscover._tcp → Microsoft Exchange/Outlook email auto-configuration
— _ldap._tcp → Active Directory / LDAP directory services

For most organisations, SRV records are sparse. When they exist, they confirm the presence of specific communication or directory services — useful context in a professional engagement.

---

**Zone Transfer: Accidentally Handing Out the Building Blueprint**

This is the most dramatic concept in DNS security. When it goes wrong, it goes spectacularly wrong.

**Why zone transfer exists**: DNS is designed with redundancy in mind. Every domain should have at least two nameservers — a primary and one or more secondaries — so that if the primary nameserver goes offline, DNS continues to work. To keep all secondary nameservers in sync with the primary, DNS uses a mechanism called a zone transfer: the secondary periodically asks the primary for a complete copy of all DNS records.

This is entirely legitimate. Zone transfers are essential for DNS reliability.

**The analogy**: Imagine the building's management office needs to maintain identical copies of the building directory at three reception desks across different floors. Every morning, the main management office sends a complete copy of the directory to each reception desk. This keeps them all in sync. The problem comes when the management office is configured to give a complete directory copy to ANYONE who asks — not just the authorised reception desks.

**What goes wrong**: Zone transfer requests (AXFR queries) should only be accepted from the authorised secondary nameservers — servers that are explicitly configured and trusted. When a nameserver is misconfigured to accept zone transfer requests from ANY IP address, any attacker — or penetration tester — can request the complete list of every DNS record in the zone.

**What a successful zone transfer reveals**:
— Every internal hostname: vpn.meridian-financial.com, db01.meridian-financial.com, jenkins.meridian-financial.com
— Every IP address for every host
— Internal naming conventions that reveal the structure of the network
— Services and servers the organisation never intended to be publicly known
— Sometimes: private IP addresses that reveal internal network segments

**How to attempt it (in an authorised engagement)**:
dig axfr @ns1.target.com target.com

If the zone transfer is misconfigured, the response contains thousands of records — a complete map of everything in DNS.

**Is this still common?** Less common than it was in the early 2000s — when open zone transfers were routine and documented by security researchers against government and corporate networks. But misconfigured zone transfers are still found today, particularly in:
— Older infrastructure managed by teams who configured nameservers years ago
— Organisations that migrated to a hosted DNS provider but kept an old self-managed nameserver running
— Internal nameservers that were never intended to face the internet directly

**The professional handling**: Always test for zone transfer on authorised engagements. If one is found, document it immediately with the exact command and output. Do NOT use the information to jump directly to active exploitation — document the finding first, assess what was revealed, and include it as a critical finding in the report. An open zone transfer is a critical security misconfiguration regardless of whether the records it reveals lead to immediate exploitation.

---

**Subdomain Enumeration: Mapping the Branches**

Even when zone transfer fails — which it should, on properly configured nameservers — subdomains can still be systematically discovered.

**What it is**: Subdomain enumeration is the process of finding every hostname registered under a domain. The main domain meridian-financial.com is the headquarters. Subdomains (dev., staging., mail., portal., api., legacy.) are the branches.

**The analogy**: If the main domain is a company's headquarters, subdomains are its branch offices and satellite facilities. Some are well-maintained and professionally managed. Some were opened years ago, forgotten, and are running with decade-old equipment. Some are still under construction and were never meant to be customer-facing. An investigator who visits only headquarters while a branch is running unpatched legacy software has found nothing of value compared to what the branch might reveal.

**Methods for subdomain enumeration**:

— **Wordlist-based brute force**: Systematically query for common subdomain names — dev, staging, mail, vpn, api, admin, portal, internal, legacy, test, old, beta, dashboard, login, remote, owa, citrix — and check which ones have DNS records. Tools: amass, subfinder, dnsrecon.

— **Certificate Transparency logs**: Every subdomain that has ever had an SSL certificate issued is logged publicly (crt.sh). Covered in Mission 1. This is the most reliable passive technique.

— **Search engine queries**: site:meridian-financial.com reveals every indexed subdomain — any page Google has ever indexed on any subdomain of the target. Covered in Mission 4.

— **Zone transfer**: When it works, it gives everything at once. Most reliable — but rarely available on properly configured nameservers.

**Why subdomains matter so much in reconnaissance**:

Development and staging environments are typically:
— Running application code that mirrors production — often less patched
— Configured with weaker access controls (because 'it's just dev')
— Not behind the CDN that protects the main site
— Not actively monitored by the security team
— Sometimes accessible from the public internet when they should not be

Forgotten subdomains are:
— Often running software from the era they were last touched
— Sometimes pointing to discontinued cloud services (dangling CNAME vulnerability)
— Not on anyone's patch management list
— Not in anyone's security team's mental model of what the organisation runs

The most significant finding in many professional engagements comes from a subdomain — not from the main website, not from active scanning, but from a hostname discovered through DNS enumeration that nobody at the target organisation was thinking about.

callouts.title: Zone Transfer Test Command
callouts.text:
In an authorised engagement, test for zone transfer with:

dig axfr @ns1.target.com target.com

Replace ns1.target.com with the actual NS record you found, and target.com with the actual domain.

If zone transfer is properly configured, you will receive:
; Transfer failed.

If it is misconfigured, you will receive a complete dump of every DNS record in the zone — hundreds or thousands of records.

IMPORTANT: Only attempt this when you have explicit written authorisation covering active DNS queries to the target's nameservers. A zone transfer request goes directly to the target's nameserver — it is an active query, not passive.

callouts.title: Zone Transfer is Active Reconnaissance
callouts.text:
Unlike reading public DNS records from a resolver, a zone transfer request goes directly to the target's nameserver. It is logged on the nameserver. It is an active technique.

The passive equivalent — Certificate Transparency logs (crt.sh) — achieves similar subdomain discovery without contacting the target's systems.

Always exhaust passive subdomain discovery (crt.sh, search engine queries, wordlist-based DNS lookups through public resolvers) before attempting zone transfer in an active phase.

keyTerms.definition: Pointer record. Maps an IP address to a hostname — the reverse of what A records do. Stored in the in-addr.arpa DNS zone. Used by mail servers for spam prevention. In reconnaissance, PTR lookups on discovered IPs reveal server roles and internal naming conventions.

Service record. Specifies which server and port handle a specific network service for a domain (VoIP via SIP, messaging via XMPP, email auto-configuration via autodiscover). Format: _service._protocol.domain → priority weight port target. Confirms the presence of specific communication or directory services.

A DNS mechanism for copying complete zone data from a primary nameserver to secondary nameservers. When misconfigured to accept requests from any IP address, it dumps every DNS record in the zone — hostnames, IPs, internal server names — to any requester. A critical security misconfiguration when exposed publicly. Active technique requiring authorisation.

The systematic process of discovering all subdomains registered under a domain. Methods: wordlist brute force, Certificate Transparency logs (crt.sh), search engine queries, and zone transfer (active). Subdomains reveal the full attack surface — including forgotten, unpatched, and CDN-bypassing servers that represent the highest-value targets in many engagements.
